additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional Disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or marked negative symptoms seen in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. Overall functioning outside the sphere of the delusional belief can be relatively preserved, and behavior is not obviously bizarre apart from the implications of the delusion. The themes of delusions are often non-bizarre (e.g., persecutory, jealous, somatic, or grandiose) and are held with strong conviction despite clear contradictory evidence. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and may be associated with stress, social isolation, or sensory/cognitive changes, and the course can be chronic with fluctuating intensity but without the pervasive deterioration seen in schizophrenia.

patient.personality: She is a warm, culturally grounded, and assertive caregiver who carefully organizes her clients’ and her own life, balancing meticulous responsibility with a passionate engagement in art, cooking, and community activities.
patient.stressor: In the past year, Olga’s household became increasingly strained when one of her adult children moved back home after a breakup, bringing financial and emotional stress into an already tight living situation. At the same time, ongoing disagreements with her husband about money management and support for extended family in Guatemala intensified, challenging her sense of control and fairness, which she usually maintained through careful budgeting and structured routines. As stress mounted, she began to interpret certain family interactions and everyday events in a very fixed way that made sense to her but clashed sharply with how others in the home saw the same situations, leading to frequent arguments and confusion. After several months in which these unshakable interpretations started to spill over into conflicts at work and with neighbors, her primary care provider, noticing how consumed she was by these specific beliefs, recommended a psychiatric evaluation at the urging of her worried daughter.
patient.chief_complaint: “Everyone keeps telling me I’m reading things wrong, but I know what’s really going on and I can’t be convinced otherwise.”

S019.manifestation: For months now, I keep seeing little things—like the way my husband closes his phone when I walk in, or how my daughter and my son lower their voices in the kitchen—and I know they’ve been meeting and planning behind my back to move money around and maybe even sell this house without telling me, no matter how many times they insist I’m imagining it.
